newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Iraq to reward friends with oil deals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Iraq to reward friends with oil deals.

text.p: Iraq's oil minister, Amir Muhammad Rasheed, made it clear on Thursday that countries which have lent political support would be favoured in doing oil business with Baghdad.

He also emphasised that he expects a quick resumption of oil exports under the United Nations "oil-for-food" deal and said he believes problems which have held up approval of aid contracts under the scheme have been smoothed out.

Rasheed, speaking at a news conference after a meeting of OPEC ministers earlier in the day, said the delay in resuming oil exports since the U.N. scheme was renewed on June 8 was due to the "normal procedures" in working out the details of Iraq's plan for procurement and distribution of aid.

"Possibly in a few days (the distribution plan) will be sent to the (U.N.) Secretary General for endorsement and approval. There is no reference to the Security Council," Rasheed explained. "That is why I have said in seven to 10 days we will start exporting oil again."
Some analysts and oil traders have expressed scepticism that Iraq will export oil that quickly.

But Rasheed said that after the distribution plan is endorsed, U.N. approval for an unchanged price formula and oil contracts with the same companies from the first period of the deal should take only a day or so.

He also said that delays in approving aid should be reduced after recent measures by the Security Council. Iraq's complaints about aid delays led to speculation that it was holding up resumption of oil exports in protest.
"The measures which were taken by the Security Council in the last few weeks are in the right direction and we hope it will be better," he said.
He said most oil companies will have renewed contracts, but the emphasis would be on those from countries which have been politically supportive.
"Friendly countries are definitely a priority when awarding new contracts. Usually, with the friendly countries whatever they want we give them, within reason," Rasheed said.

Oil executives who had met with the head of Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) in Vienna said they expected some existing contract holders might get cut back in order to leave more for Russian companies.
Russia has been one of Iraq's strongest supporters in its efforts to have sanctions eased.
Russian companies accounted for the largest block of oil under the first period of the "oil-for-food" deal, lifting around 23.5 percent of a total of nearly 120 million barrels.
"They are talking about cutting some people back to give more to the Russians," said an executive from a company with a contract to lift Iraqi oil.

Iraq also is linking its 10 lucrative upstream development deals to political support. Already, the $3.5 billion project to develop the West Qurna oilfield, with estimated production capacity of 600,000 bpd, has gone to three Russian companies. Russia is also seen as favoured for at least two others.

A deal was recently signed with China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC) for the Ahdab field, which Rasheed said had a forecast production rate of 100,000 bpd and CNPC appears close to being awarded a deal to develop Halfaya, with an estimated production rate of 250,000 bpd.
"We are in a very good position on Halfaya with the Chinese," Rasheed said.
Western European countries like France, Spain and Italy also ranked high on the list of preferred partners, he said.
"We are at a quite advanced stage and there are very fruitful discussions with the governments as well as the companies (in those countries)," he said.
-- Vienna newsroom +431 713 2002
